meta.titre: Ionisation Energy: Reading Successive Values and Explaining Trends

sections.contenu_markdown: When a bar of magnesium ribbon flares up in a laboratory at Bamenda, atoms of the metal are giving up electrons to oxygen, and how easily they do so is measured by ionisation energy. The same quantity explains why sodium and potassium from the school store must be kept under oil while magnesium can sit on a shelf, and why the metals in group 1 form 1+ ions while those in group 2 form 2+ ions. Examiners use tables of successive ionisation energies to ask you to find the group of an unknown element, so this topic rewards anyone who can read the numbers and explain them with shells, shielding and nuclear charge.

items: An atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons in shells and subshells (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p).
The number of protons in the nucleus is the atomic number, and a neutral atom has the same number of electrons.
Electrons in inner shells reduce the pull of the nucleus on outer electrons; this is called shielding.
One mole of a substance contains $6.02\times10^{23}$ particles, and energy changes are quoted in kJ per mole.

sections.titre: Ionisation energy: definition, successive values and trends
sections.contenu_markdown:
The **first ionisation energy** of an element is the energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous ions with a single positive charge. It is measured in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. For an element X: $\mathrm{X(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{X^{+}(g)} + e^{-}$

The state symbols (g) are part of the definition. The **second ionisation energy** refers to the next electron, removed from the gaseous 1+ ion: for example $\mathrm{Mg^{+}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mg^{2+}(g)} + e^{-}$

**Three factors** control the size of an ionisation energy:

1. **Nuclear charge.** More protons attract the electrons more strongly, so the energy rises.
2. **Atomic radius.** The further the outer electron is from the nucleus, the weaker the attraction, so the energy falls.
3. **Shielding.** Inner electrons repel the outer electron, reducing the effective pull of the nucleus; more shielding lowers the energy.

**Successive ionisation energies always increase**, because each electron is removed from an ion with a larger positive charge and the same nuclear charge, so the remaining electrons are held more tightly. A **very large jump** occurs when the next electron comes from an inner shell, which is closer to the nucleus and less shielded. The number of electrons removed before the big jump equals the number of outer-shell electrons, which gives the group number.

**Trends.** Down a group the first ionisation energy falls, since the outer electron is in a shell further out and is shielded by more inner shells (for group 1: Li 520, Na 496, K 419, all in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$). Across a period it rises generally, since the nuclear charge increases while the electrons enter the same shell and the shielding stays almost constant.

variantes.nom: Successive ionisation energies and the group
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a list of consecutive ionisation energies is given and you must find the group or the formula of an ion.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Look for the largest ratio between neighbouring values, not simply the largest value. If the big jump follows the $n$th ionisation energy, the element has $n$ outer electrons: it is in group $n$ (groups 1 and 2) or group $n + 10$ (groups 13 to 18). A metal forms an ion of charge $n+$; a non-metal gains $8 - n$ electrons and forms an ion of charge $(8-n)-$. The total energy to form a 2+ ion from gaseous atoms is the **sum** of the first two values.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked why a first ionisation energy falls at a certain element, for example between beryllium and boron or between nitrogen and oxygen.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Boron (801) is lower than beryllium (900) because its outer electron is in a 2p subshell, which is higher in energy and further from the nucleus than the 2s subshell, and is partly shielded by the 2s electrons. Oxygen (1314) is lower than nitrogen (1402) because one 2p orbital of oxygen holds a pair of electrons; the repulsion between the two electrons in the same orbital makes one of them easier to remove. The same pattern occurs at aluminium and sulphur in period 3.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When comparing two elements in the same group, or explaining the reactivity of group 1 or group 2 metals.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Group 2 first ionisation energies fall from Be (900) to Mg (738) to Ca (590). The outer electrons are in shells that are further out and more shielded, so they are lost more easily and the metals are more reactive. The effect of the larger nuclear charge is outweighed by the extra shell and shielding.

sections.enonce_markdown:
The table gives the successive ionisation energies, in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, of two elements D and E. The letters are not chemical symbols.

| Element | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th | 5th | 6th |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| D | 738 | 1451 | 7733 | 10540 | 13630 | not given |
| E | 1012 | 1907 | 2914 | 4964 | 6274 | 21267 |

(a) State the group of D and of E, giving your reasoning.

(b) Deduce the formula of the ionic compound formed between D and E.

(c) Calculate the energy needed to convert 0.0200 mol of gaseous atoms of D into gaseous $\mathrm{D^{2+}}$ ions.

(d) Explain why the jump for D is so much larger than the others.

etapes.action: Find the largest ratio in the data for D.
etapes.justification: The big jump marks the point where electrons start to come from an inner shell.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Ratios: $\dfrac{1451}{738} = 1.97$, $\dfrac{7733}{1451} = 5.33$, $\dfrac{10540}{7733} = 1.36$. The jump follows the **2nd** value, so D has 2 outer electrons: **group 2**.

etapes.justification: The number of values before the big jump gives the number of outer electrons.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The ratios are close to 1.3 to 1.9 until $\dfrac{21267}{6274} = 3.39$ after the **5th** value. E has 5 outer electrons: **group 15**.

etapes.action: Work out the ions and the formula.
etapes.justification: D loses 2 electrons to form $\mathrm{D^{2+}}$. E, with 5 outer electrons, gains 3 to complete its octet and forms $\mathrm{E^{3-}}$. Charges must cancel, so 3 D ions (+6) balance 2 E ions (-6).

etapes.action: Calculate the energy for the 2+ ion.
etapes.justification: Forming $\mathrm{D^{2+}}$ from the gaseous atom needs the first and second ionisations, so their values are added: $\mathrm{D(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{D^{2+}(g)} + 2e^{-}$
The third electron is not an outer electron.
etapes.resultat_markdown: After two electrons are removed, the third must come from the inner full shell, which is closer to the nucleus and is shielded by fewer electrons, so it is held much more strongly by the same nuclear charge.

sections.conclusion_markdown: D is in group 2 and E in group 15; they form $\mathrm{D_3E_2}$, and 43.8 kJ is needed to ionise 0.0200 mol of D atoms twice.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing the first ionisation equation as $\mathrm{Na(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na^{+}(s)} + e^{-}$
items.pourquoi_faux: The definition applies to gaseous atoms and gives gaseous ions. Removing an electron from a solid involves other energy terms such as atomisation.
items.correction_markdown: The correct equation is $\mathrm{Na(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na^{+}(g)} + e^{-}$ with (g) on both sides.

items.erreur_markdown: "The second ionisation energy is smaller than the first, because the ion is smaller and has fewer electrons to repel."
items.pourquoi_faux: Removing an electron from a positive ion is harder. The nuclear charge is unchanged but there is one electron fewer, so the remaining electrons are pulled closer and held more tightly.
items.correction_markdown: Successive ionisation energies **always increase**: for magnesium 738 then 1451 $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

items.erreur_markdown: "The big jump comes after the 3rd value, so the element is in group 4."
items.pourquoi_faux: The element has as many outer electrons as there are values before the jump, and its group follows from that number, not from the number of the next value.
items.correction_markdown: Three values before the jump means 3 outer electrons: **group 13** (the group of aluminium), not group 4.

items.erreur_markdown: "The first ionisation energy of boron is lower than that of beryllium because boron has a bigger atomic radius."
items.pourquoi_faux: Boron is smaller than beryllium. The real reason is that the outer electron of boron is in a 2p subshell, higher in energy and partly shielded by the 2s electrons.
items.correction_markdown: Boron: 2p electron removed more easily than the 2s electron of beryllium, so 801 is below 900 $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

items.erreur_markdown: "Ionisation energy is the energy to remove an electron from an atom."
items.pourquoi_faux: The definition is incomplete: it does not say which electron, the amount of substance, or the state, so it would earn no mark.
items.correction_markdown: Say: the energy to remove **one mole of electrons** from **one mole of gaseous atoms** to form **one mole of gaseous 1+ ions**.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Write the equation, with state symbols, for the second ionisation energy of calcium.

(b) State, with a reason, which element has the higher first ionisation energy in each pair: calcium or strontium; potassium or sodium.

(c) Write the equation for the third ionisation energy of aluminium.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\mathrm{Ca^{+}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ca^{2+}(g)} + e^{-}$

(b) **Calcium** is higher than strontium: strontium's outer electrons are in a shell further from the nucleus and are shielded by an extra shell. **Sodium** is higher than potassium for the same reason.

(c) $\mathrm{Al^{2+}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Al^{3+}(g)} + e^{-}$

items.enonce_markdown:
An element Z has the first five ionisation energies $590$, $1145$, $4912$, $6491$ and $8153\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

(a) State the group of Z and the formula of its ion.

(b) Calculate the energy needed to convert 0.250 mol of gaseous Z atoms into gaseous $\mathrm{Z^{2+}}$ ions.

(c) Write the equation for the second ionisation energy of Z and explain why the third value is so much larger.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The ratios are $\dfrac{1145}{590} = 1.94$ and $\dfrac{4912}{1145} = 4.29$, the largest, after the 2nd value. Z has 2 outer electrons: **group 2**, ion $\mathrm{Z^{2+}}$.

(b) $590 + 1145 = 1735\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, so $E = 0.250\times1735 = 433.75\ \mathrm{kJ} \approx \mathbf{434\ kJ}$.

(c) $\mathrm{Z^{+}(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Z^{2+}(g)} + e^{-}$ The third electron comes from the inner full shell, closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so it needs far more energy.

items.enonce_markdown:
The first ionisation energies of the elements of period 3, in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, are:

| Na | Mg | Al | Si | P | S | Cl | Ar |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 496 | 738 | 578 | 786 | 1012 | 1000 | 1251 | 1521 |

(a) Identify the two elements whose values break the general upward trend.

(b) Explain each of these two exceptions.

(c) Calculate the energy needed to remove the first two electrons from every atom in 6.0 g of gaseous magnesium atoms ($\mathrm{Mg} = 24.0$; second ionisation energy $1451\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$).
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Aluminium** (578 is below 738 for magnesium) and **sulphur** (1000 is below 1012 for phosphorus).

(b) Aluminium: the outer electron is in a 3p subshell, which is higher in energy and further from the nucleus than 3s, and is partly shielded by the 3s electrons, so it is easier to remove than a 3s electron of magnesium. Sulphur: its configuration is $3p^4$, so one 3p orbital holds a pair of electrons; repulsion between them makes one electron easier to remove than the unpaired 3p electron of phosphorus.

(c) $n = \dfrac{6.0}{24.0} = 0.25\ \mathrm{mol}$. Energy per mole $= 738 + 1451 = 2189\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, so $E = 0.25\times2189 = 547.25\ \mathrm{kJ} \approx \mathbf{547\ kJ}$.

items_markdown: First ionisation energy: energy to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms, giving gaseous 1+ ions; always write state symbols.
Three factors: nuclear charge (raises it), atomic radius and shielding (lower it).
Successive ionisation energies always rise; a very large jump shows that the next electron comes from an inner shell, so the number of values before the jump is the group number.
Across a period the value rises generally, with dips at the start of a new subshell (B, Al) and where electrons first pair in a p orbital (O, S).
Down a group the value falls because the outer electron is further out and more shielded, so metals become more reactive.
The energy to form a 2+ ion from gaseous atoms is the sum of the first two ionisation energies.
